description: We’re a team of curious students from Kyrgyzstan passionate about robotics, AI, and 3D modeling. We love building things that work, from code to hardware. We’re looking for teammates who bring skills in data analysis, Python, web or app development, or design and presentation. No matter your level, if you’re motivated and ready to learn, join us and let’s build something out of this world!
summary:
TRACE is an interactive web platform that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into a clear picture of how the surface changes and who is exposed to it. We developed it around a case study in Kyrgyzstan: the Toguz-Bulak landslide (about 42,800 m³ of material, 11 people evacuated, a road and a power substation under threat).

The site combines NISAR GCOV and GUNW products with IMERG rainfall and HLS optical imagery. Users can scrub through time with Earth Time Machine, compare optical and radar views with Radar Vision, and run Earth Impact, which counts nearby settlements, roads and buildings and generates an investigation report. Every layer comes with a Data & Science page that states the methodology and the limits of the data. SAR detects surface change, not underground processes.

TRACE addresses the challenge by making SAR data readable for people without remote-sensing training, such as local authorities, emergency teams and students. This matters because mountain regions like Kyrgyzstan face frequent landslides, and rain, ground change and exposed infrastructure are rarely seen together. The same approach can be applied to any region NISAR covers.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
TRACE is an interactive web platform that shows how the Earth’s surface changes and who is exposed to it. The user opens a map of Kyrgyzstan and zooms to the Toguz-Bulak landslide. Earth Time Machine is a timeline (September to November) that plays back NISAR observations together with IMERG rainfall. Radar Vision lets the user switch between optical (HLS) and radar views of the same place. Earth Impact counts the settlements, roads, buildings and natural events within a chosen radius and generates an investigation report. A Data & Science section explains the methodology and the limits of the data.
Benefits.
TRACE makes SAR data understandable to people without remote-sensing training, such as local authorities, emergency teams, students and journalists. It puts ground change, rainfall and exposed infrastructure in one place, so users can see the context of a hazard without switching between specialist tools.
Intended impact.
We want to give mountain communities a clearer view of landslide risk and help decision-makers decide where to look first. We built it around Kyrgyzstan, where landslides are frequent, but the approach works anywhere NISAR collects data.
Tools and technologies.
Data: NISAR GCOV and GUNW products, NASA IMERG precipitation, HLS optical imagery
Web: Web: TypeScript (strict), React 19, Vite 8; MapLibre GL JS 6 for the interactive map (Esri Dark Gray basemap), custom SVG time-series chart.
Hosting: GitHub Pages
Design and collaboration: claude ,Invideo
Hardware: none. We chose a simulation-only, fully interactive project.
How is it creative?
Instead of showing raw radar images, TRACE turns them into a story the user can explore: scrub through time, switch between radar and optical, and finish with a report.If Listen to Earth was built: it also turns surface change into sound. The project presents the data honestly, including what it cannot show.
What factors did we consider?
Scientific honesty: SAR detects surface change, not underground processes, so we state this openly and do not claim more than the data supports.
Audience: the interface had to be usable by non-experts.
Local relevance: the case study comes from Kyrgyzstan but the method applies globally.
Limits: we show the methodology and the limitations of the data and the detector in the Data & Science section.
Time: we prioritised real data first, then interface, then extra features.
